subject: chemistry
promptStrong: Give me a challenging GCSE exam-style question on exothermic/endothermic reactions and bond energy calculations, then mark my answer against the Eduqas spec.
promptWeak: Explain exothermic and endothermic reactions and bond energy calculations for GCSE Eduqas Chemistry simply, with a worked example and the most common mistake.

questions.q: Which statement correctly describes an exothermic reaction?
options: It takes in energy from the surroundings
It transfers energy to the surroundings
It causes no change in temperature
It only happens in living cells
questions.explain: An exothermic reaction transfers (releases) energy to the surroundings, so the temperature of the surroundings rises.

questions.q: During a reaction the temperature of the surroundings falls. What does this tell you?
questions.explain: A fall in the temperature of the surroundings means energy has been taken in from them, so the reaction is endothermic.

questions.q: Which of these is an example of an endothermic process?
options: Neutralising an acid with an alkali
Thermal decomposition of a metal carbonate
questions.explain: Thermal decomposition (e.g. of a carbonate) takes in energy, so it is endothermic. Combustion, neutralisation and crystallising hand warmers are exothermic.

questions.q: In an exothermic reaction, what happens to the temperature of the surroundings?
questions.explain: Exothermic reactions release energy to the surroundings, so the surroundings get hotter and the temperature rises.

questions.q: On a reaction profile for an exothermic reaction, where are the products relative to the reactants?
options: At a higher energy level than the reactants
At the same energy level as the reactants
At a lower energy level than the reactants
questions.explain: In an exothermic reaction energy is released, so the products sit at a lower energy level than the reactants on the reaction profile.

questions.q: On a reaction profile for an endothermic reaction, where are the products relative to the reactants?
options: At a lower energy level than the reactants
At the same level as the reactants
At a higher energy level than the reactants
questions.explain: In an endothermic reaction energy is taken in, so the products are at a higher energy level than the reactants.

questions.q: On a reaction profile, which quantity is shown by the 'hump' measured from the reactants up to the peak?
options: The bond energy of the products
questions.explain: The height from the reactants to the top of the curve is the activation energy, the minimum energy needed for the reaction to occur.

questions.q: What is meant by the activation energy of a reaction?
options: The energy released when products form
The total energy of the reactants
The energy stored in the products
The minimum energy needed for a reaction to occur
questions.explain: Activation energy is the minimum energy that colliding particles must have for a reaction to take place.

questions.q: Which statement about bonds during a reaction is correct?
options: Breaking bonds releases energy; making bonds takes in energy
Breaking bonds takes in energy; making bonds releases energy
Both breaking and making bonds release energy
Both breaking and making bonds take in energy
questions.explain: Breaking bonds is endothermic (energy taken in); making new bonds is exothermic (energy released). The balance determines the overall energy change.

questions.q: A reaction releases more energy making bonds than it takes in breaking bonds. The reaction is therefore:
questions.explain: If more energy is released forming bonds than is used breaking them, the reaction gives out energy overall, so it is exothermic.

questions.q: Which expression gives the overall energy change of a reaction from bond energies?
options: Energy of bonds made minus energy of bonds broken
Energy of bonds broken minus energy of bonds made
Energy of bonds broken plus energy of bonds made
Energy of bonds made divided by bonds broken
questions.explain: Overall energy change = (sum of bond energies broken) - (sum of bond energies made). A negative result means exothermic.

questions.q: A reaction breaks bonds needing 900 kJ and makes bonds releasing 1000 kJ. What is the overall energy change?
questions.explain: Energy change = bonds broken - bonds made = 900 - 1000 = -100 kJ. The negative value shows the reaction is exothermic.

questions.q: For H2 + Cl2 -> 2HCl, bonds broken need 436 (H-H) + 242 (Cl-Cl) = 678 kJ, and 2 H-Cl bonds made release 2 x 431 = 862 kJ. What is the overall energy change?
questions.explain: Energy change = bonds broken - bonds made = 678 - 862 = -184 kJ. The negative sign means the reaction is exothermic.

questions.q: A bond energy calculation gives an overall value of +55 kJ. What does the positive sign indicate?
questions.explain: A positive overall energy change means more energy was used breaking bonds than was released making them, so the reaction is endothermic.

questions.q: What happens to a simple chemical cell over time as it is used?
options: It produces a potential difference until the reactants are used up
It produces a constant potential difference forever
It never produces any potential difference
questions.explain: A chemical cell produces a potential difference from a chemical reaction, and it continues until the reactants are used up.

questions.q: What is the only product formed when a hydrogen-oxygen fuel cell operates?
questions.explain: In a hydrogen-oxygen fuel cell hydrogen reacts with oxygen and the only product is water, which is why it is a clean source of energy.

questions.q: Which is a genuine advantage of a hydrogen-oxygen fuel cell over a petrol engine?
options: Hydrogen is always cheaper and easier to store
It never needs a supply of fuel
It produces only water at the point of use, so no carbon dioxide there
questions.explain: A key advantage is that the fuel cell produces only water at the point of use, so no carbon dioxide is released there. Storing hydrogen safely is actually a disadvantage.

questions.q: Which is a genuine disadvantage of hydrogen fuel cells for cars?
options: They release large amounts of carbon dioxide
Hydrogen is difficult and potentially dangerous to store and transport
They cannot produce a potential difference
questions.explain: A real disadvantage is that hydrogen is a flammable gas that is hard to store and transport safely. Fuel cells do not emit carbon dioxide at the point of use.

questions.q: In specified practical SP8, the amount of energy released by a fuel is found by using the burning fuel to heat a known mass of what?
questions.explain: The fuel heats a known mass of water; the temperature rise of the water is used to work out the energy released by the fuel.

questions.q: In the fuel calorimetry practical, which change would make the measured energy released appear lower than the true value?
options: Insulating the container of water very well
Using a lid to reduce evaporation
Stirring the water to spread the heat evenly
Heat lost to the surroundings instead of to the water
questions.explain: Heat lost to the surroundings rather than to the water means the water warms less, so the calculated energy released is lower than the true value. Insulation, a lid and stirring all reduce this loss.
